claims.label: issue (blocking)
claims.subject: Word-pair key is case-sensitive, so the same pair gets two different keys depending on sentence position
claims.discussion:
Word-pair key is case-sensitive, so the same pair gets two different keys depending on sentence position. Introduced by this change. `ExtractWordPairFromText` builds the canonical key from the raw `token.Form` and `token.Misc.IncorrectForm`. I traced `Form` in `services/ai-guide/models/universal_dependency_types.go` (lines 51-80): it is the literal surface form — `ReconstructSentence` concatenates `Form` verbatim to rebuild the sentence, and the existing tests in `universal_dependency_types_test.go` use `Form: "Hello"` / `IncorrectForm: "Hallo"`, i.e. capitalization is preserved exactly as it appears in the sentence.

So when the confused word lands at the start of a sentence the pair canonicalizes differently from the identical pair mid-sentence, and the ASCII sort makes it worse rather than better: mid-sentence you get `sort("accept","except") = "accept|except"`, but sentence-initially you get `sort("Except","accept")` — 'E' (0x45) sorts before 'a' (0x61) — so `"Except|accept"`. Same pair, two keys, and even the operand order flips.

Concrete failure: a student answers an FCW item on accept/except correctly twice, but one of the two sentences began with the word. `_computeCorrectPairs` records `"accept|except": 1` and `"Except|accept": 1`; neither reaches `_masteryThreshold = 2`, so `ComputeProvenWordPairs` returns nothing and `GetUnseenChallenge` happily serves the mastered pair again — exactly the repetition this PR exists to prevent. The same mismatch silently defeats the `avoidPairs` check at `langlit_challenge_component.go:1059-1060`, since the freshly generated dependency output is canonicalized the same way.

This matters more than a normal logic slip because the key is now *persisted*: `CreateLanglitAttempt` writes `WordPair` onto an immutable `WrittenOnceModel`, so mixed-case keys written before a fix stay wrong and would need a re-migration to repair. Worth fixing before this lands.

Fix: lowercase both forms before sorting and joining (note `strings` is not currently imported in this file — the import needs adding).
claims.failure_scenario: Word-pair key is case-sensitive, so the same pair gets two different keys depending on sentence position

claims.label: issue (blocking)
claims.subject: Assignment-scoped backfill materializes an unbounded set of challenges and rewrites them on the render path
claims.discussion:
Assignment-scoped backfill materializes an unbounded set of challenges and rewrites them on the render path. Introduced by this change. `_backfillLanglitAttempts` issues `GetMulti` over one key per cold attempt and then `PutMulti` over the same set, with nothing bounding that set on the assignment path. The two scoping branches are asymmetric: the `else` branch at line 211 deliberately caps at `_provenScopeSize = 15` ("take a bounded recent window"), but the `assignmentID != ""` branch at lines 203-208 appends *every* attempt matching the assignment with no cap. Its input is `previousAttempts` from `GetLanglitAttemptsOrdered`, which I read at handlers.go:433-467 — it uses `ds_helpers.ReadAllResourcePages`, i.e. the student's entire attempt history with no limit.

I checked the batch limits before claiming a hard failure: `pkg/gcloud/datastore/client.go` splits `PutMulti` at `MaxWriteBatchSize = 500` and `GetMulti` at `batchSize = 200`, so this will not error out on volume. The defect is therefore cost and latency, not a crash — but it is on the synchronous path that renders a challenge for a student, and it scales with a user-controlled quantity. At 100x the data (a long-running assignment, or an assignment id reused across a course) a single render fans out into hundreds of datastore reads plus hundreds of writes before the student sees anything.

The expected shape here is the one the `else` branch already uses: cap the assignment-scoped set the same way (or backfill at most one bounded batch per invocation and let repeat visits finish the migration — the migration is explicitly designed to be lazy and incremental, so processing a bounded slice per request is the fix, not a regression).
claims.failure_scenario: Assignment-scoped backfill materializes an unbounded set of challenges and rewrites them on the render path

claims.label: issue (blocking)
claims.subject: Attempts that can never be warmed are re-classified as cold and re-migrated on every single request
claims.discussion:
Attempts that can never be warmed are re-classified as cold and re-migrated on every single request. Introduced by this change. The classification switch treats "cold" as `default` — i.e. anything that is neither (`WordPair != "" && type matches`) nor (`type set && type differs`). Two categories fall into `default` permanently, so the lazy migration never converges for them:

1. **Challenge missing.** Lines 310-313 skip an attempt whose challenge was deleted or archived and leave it cold by design. On the next request that attempt is `default` again, so its key is re-added to the `GetMulti` at line 298 — forever, once per render.
2. **Legitimately empty pair.** An attempt whose `ChallengeType` *equals* `challengeType` but whose `WordPair` is `""` fails case 1 (empty pair) and fails case 2 (types are equal), so it lands in `default`. The backfill then writes it back with `WordPair = ""` (line 316/325) and the next request classifies it as cold again — and this one costs a `PutMulti` write, not just a read, on every render. This is not hypothetical: the doc comment the PR adds at `models/langlit_challenge.go:309-312` states outright that "a challenge with no IncorrectForm token legitimately yields ''".

I checked whether case 2 is reachable for freshly generated content: `isValidDependencyOutput` (`langlit_challenge_component.go:536-542`) does require at least one token with a non-empty `IncorrectForm`, so newly generated challenges are safe. That guard does not cover challenges written before it existed, nor the deleted-challenge path, which is unconditional.

Effect: a steady per-request datastore read (and, for category 2, write) amplification that the "improve in performance over time" story in the PR description assumes away. The fix is to make "already attempted migration" distinguishable from "never attempted" — e.g. treat `ChallengeType != ""` as warm regardless of `WordPair`, and record a sentinel (or skip re-queuing) for attempts whose challenge could not be hydrated.
claims.failure_scenario: Attempts that can never be warmed are re-classified as cold and re-migrated on every single request

claims.label: suggestion (non-blocking)
claims.subject: The 15-attempt recent window is applied before type filtering, so unassigned practice rarely accumulates a proven pair
claims.discussion:
The 15-attempt recent window is applied before type filtering, so unassigned practice rarely accumulates a proven pair. Introduced by this change. For unassigned practice the scope is `attempts[:min(len, 15)]` taken from `GetLanglitAttemptsOrdered`, which I confirmed at handlers.go:448-451 filters only on `user_kaid` and orders by `-created_at` — it is *not* type-scoped. Type scoping then happens afterwards, inside the counting loop.

So the window is 15 attempts across all langlit challenge types. `challengeTypes` in the component covers frequently-confused-words, apostrophe usage, subject-verb agreement, its-vs-its, verb forms and pronoun-antecedent agreement; a student rotating among them contributes only a couple of same-type attempts to any 15-attempt window. Reaching `_masteryThreshold = 2` corrects *on the same pair* within that residue is unlikely, so `ComputeProvenWordPairs` returns empty and the cached-challenge skip at line 411 is a no-op for most unassigned practice — the very case the constant's comment says it is sizing for.

Taking the most recent 15 attempts *of the requested type* (filter first, then window) would make the bound mean what the comment claims it means, at no extra cost since the full list is already in memory.
claims.failure_scenario: The 15-attempt recent window is applied before type filtering, so unassigned practice rarely accumulates a proven pair

claims.label: suggestion (non-blocking)
claims.subject: The pair-avoidance regeneration comment claims the avoid list is "emphasized", but the retry sends byte-identical prompt inputs
claims.discussion:
The pair-avoidance regeneration comment claims the avoid list is "emphasized", but the retry sends byte-identical prompt inputs. Introduced by this change. The `continue` is commented "regenerate with the avoid list emphasized", but I traced every value in the parameter map at lines 966-978 and none of them changes between iterations: `previousSentence`, `previousNouns`, `correctForm`/`incorrectForm` and `themeSteering` are all computed before the loop starts, and `avoidPairs` is computed once at line 836 and never mutated. `pairAvoidRegens` is not passed to the model. The retry is therefore a pure re-roll that relies entirely on sampling nondeterminism, not an escalation.

That is a defensible design, but the comment asserts behavior the code does not implement, which is the kind of comment that misleads the next reader into thinking the escalation exists. Either drop the "emphasized" claim, or actually escalate — e.g. append the colliding pair to the avoid list for the retry, which costs nothing and makes the second attempt strictly more informed than the first.

Worth noting the cost side too, since it is invisible from the diff: each `continue` re-runs generation, classification and up to three dependency-generation LLM calls, so a collision roughly doubles the model spend for that request.
claims.failure_scenario: The pair-avoidance regeneration comment claims the avoid list is "emphasized", but the retry sends byte-identical prompt inputs

claims.label: suggestion (non-blocking)
claims.subject: Two new behavior branches ship with no test coverage: the unassigned recent-window scope and the pair-avoid regeneration loop
claims.discussion:
Two new behavior branches ship with no test coverage: the unassigned recent-window scope and the pair-avoid regeneration loop. Introduced by this change. The PR adds eight tests, which cover the warm/cold, threshold, assignment-scope and type-scope behavior of `_computeCorrectPairs` well. Two branches are not exercised at all:

1. **The `assignmentID == ""` recent-window branch** (`handlers.go:209-213`). Every new test in `handlers_test.go` — `TestComputeProvenWordPairs_RequiresTwoCorrects`, `_CumulativeAcrossWrongs`, `_AssignmentScope`, `_TypeScoped`, `_LazyBackfill`, `_ApostropheCounted`, and both `ComputeSeenCorrectPairs` tests — passes a non-empty `assignmentID`. `_provenScopeSize` is never exercised, so neither the truncation nor the `min` boundary is covered, and the type-mixing weakness described in the `window-before-type-filter` finding would not be caught by the suite.

2. **The `pairAvoidRegens` loop** in this file. It is the largest behavioral addition in the diff — a new outer retry wrapping generation, classification and dependency generation — and there is no test asserting that a collision triggers exactly one regeneration, that the budget relaxes after `pairAvoidMaxRegens`, or that non-word-pair types break out on the first pass. A regression that turned the `break` at line 1064 into an unbounded loop, or that inverted the `slices.Contains` check, would ship green.

A table test over `_computeCorrectPairs` with an empty `assignmentID` and >15 attempts, plus a component test with a stubbed generator that returns a colliding pair once and a fresh pair on the retry, would close both.
claims.failure_scenario: Two new behavior branches ship with no test coverage: the unassigned recent-window scope and the pair-avoid regeneration loop

claims.label: issue (blocking, best-practice)
claims.subject: Datastore: the lazy backfill writes back attempts that were read from Datastore, which this model's `WrittenOnceModel` policy forbids; copying into a fresh struct hides the check instead of changing the policy.
claims.discussion:
Datastore: the lazy backfill writes back attempts that were read from Datastore, which this model's `WrittenOnceModel` policy forbids; copying into a fresh struct hides the check instead of changing the policy. `references/entities.md` (Transaction-safety policies) states the contract for this policy: "`WrittenOnceModel` | Insert-only entities you never read-modify-write (e.g. append-only log rows). | A brand-new entity may be written with no transaction. Writing back an entity that was **read from Datastore** errors (use `WrittenInTransactionModel` if you need that)."

`LanglitChallengeAttempt.TransactionSafetyPolicy()` still returns `datastore.WrittenOnceModel` (services/ai-guide/models/langlit_challenge.go:316-318, unchanged by this PR), yet the new code does exactly the read-modify-write the policy rules out: the attempts passed to `_backfillLanglitAttempts` come from `GetLanglitAttemptsOrdered` (handlers.go:447-456, a `NewQuery(models.LanglitChallengeAttemptKind)` read — I traced the call chain `LanglitChallengeComponent` → `ComputeProvenWordPairs` → `_computeCorrectPairs` → `_backfillLanglitAttempts`), and the diff writes them back with `if _, err := ctx.Datastore().PutMulti(ctx, putKeys, putAttempts); err != nil {`. The added comment says the bypass is deliberate: "Fresh (not read-from-datastore) entities are used because LanglitChallengeAttempt is a WrittenOnceModel, which forbids writing an entity that was read from datastore."

The skill names the remedy for wanting read-modify-write: use `WrittenInTransactionModel` and do the hydrate-and-write inside one `RunInTransaction` (note the skill's warning that the closure must be idempotent, since `dstest` forces a retry). If the write-back isn't worth a transaction, the alternative that keeps the declared policy honest is to drop the persistence and compute the pair from the hydrated challenge in memory. What should not stay is a model that advertises insert-only while the read path mutates it.
claims.failure_scenario: Every langlit challenge fetch now re-Puts already-stored `LanglitChallengeAttempt` entities outside any transaction while the model still declares `WrittenOnceModel`, so the wrapper's lost-update protection is disabled for a kind whose declared contract says it is insert-only — a concurrent or later writer of the same attempt key is silently last-write-wins, and the fresh-struct copy zeroes any attempt property it forgets to carry over.

claims.label: suggestion (non-blocking, best-practice)
claims.subject: Datastore: the new `challenge_type` and `word_pair` attempt properties are never filtered or sorted on, so they should carry `noindex`.
claims.discussion:
Datastore: the new `challenge_type` and `word_pair` attempt properties are never filtered or sorted on, so they should carry `noindex`. `references/entities.md` (Struct tags) says: "`noindex` — store the value without indexing it. Use this for any field you never filter or sort on; indexed properties cost more and are capped in size."

The two new fields are declared without it:

```go
ChallengeType LanglitChallengeType `datastore:"challenge_type"`
...
WordPair string `datastore:"word_pair"`
```

I checked whether anything queries them: `grep -rn "word_pair\|challenge_type" services/ai-guide` finds exactly one `FilterField("challenge_type", ...)` (handlers.go:362) and it is on the `LanglitChallenge` kind, not on `LanglitChallengeAttempt`; the only `LanglitChallengeAttempt` query is `FilterField("user_kaid", ...).Order("-created_at")`, and `services/ai-guide/index.yaml` has no attempt index mentioning the new properties. All of the new filtering (`_computeCorrectPairs`) is in-memory. Adding `,noindex` to both tags keeps them out of the index while preserving the stored values.
claims.failure_scenario: `challenge_type` and `word_pair` are written as indexed properties on every attempt of a high-volume append-only kind (and again on every lazy backfill re-Put), paying extra index-write cost and index storage for properties no query ever filters or sorts on.

claims.subject: The three langlit config JSONs silently drop the 30–50 "Practice Items" options (cap 50 → 25); was this an intended part of the word-pair work, and what happens to assignments already saved at those values?
claims.discussion:
The three langlit config JSONs silently drop the 30–50 "Practice Items" options (cap 50 → 25); was this an intended part of the word-pair work, and what happens to assignments already saved at those values? All three `.json` config files in this PR delete the same five `options` entries (30/35/40/45/50) from the `langlit-*-iterations` SINGLE_SELECT — see the identical hunks at `langlit-frequently-confused-words.json`, `langlit-apostrophe-usage.json`, and `langlit-subject-verb-agreement.json`, each leaving `5, 10, 15, 20, 25`. claims.label: suggestion (non-blocking)
claims.subject: Cold attempts whose challenge is missing (or yields an empty word pair) are never written back, so they re-hydrate on every request forever instead of migrating lazily as the description promises.
claims.discussion:
Cold attempts whose challenge is missing (or yields an empty word pair) are never written back, so they re-hydrate on every request forever instead of migrating lazily as the description promises. The PR description states "the actual migration is done lazily... we never need to run an actual migration, because the data will be seamlessly upgraded and improve in performance over time." Two paths never reach that steady state.

1. In `_backfillLanglitAttempts`, when `challenge == nil` (line 310–313) the attempt is skipped with `continue`, so no key is appended to `putKeys`. Nothing marks the attempt as processed, so `_computeCorrectPairs` classifies it into the `default:` (cold) branch again on the next call and `GetMulti` re-fetches the missing key every time.

2. The `default:` branch at line 228 is also reached for a warm attempt whose `ChallengeType` matches but whose `WordPair` is `""`. `models.ExtractWordPair` returns `""` when no token carries an `IncorrectForm`, and the model comment you added on `WordPair` (langlit_challenge.go:309-312) explicitly acknowledges "a challenge with no IncorrectForm token legitimately yields ''". `isValidDependencyOutput` (entry_components/langlit_challenge_component.go:537-541) only guarantees this for newly generated challenges, not for ones cached before that validation existed. Such attempts are re-hydrated and re-written on every request.

A persisted "migration attempted" signal (e.g. writing `ChallengeType` alone, or a sentinel `WordPair`) would let both cases settle.
claims.failure_scenario: A student whose in-scope attempt points at a challenge that has since been deleted (or at a word-pair-type challenge with no IncorrectForm token) keeps that attempt permanently "cold": every subsequent langlit challenge request re-runs the datastore `GetMulti` hydration for it and never writes the fields back, so the "lazily migrated, improves in performance over time" claim never comes true for those attempts.

claims.label: issue (blocking)
claims.subject: Empty WordPair is used as the "needs migration" sentinel, but it is also a legitimate warm value, so those attempts never converge and are re-hydrated and re-written on every request.
claims.discussion:
Empty WordPair is used as the "needs migration" sentinel, but it is also a legitimate warm value, so those attempts never converge and are re-hydrated and re-written on every request. The switch at handlers.go:221-231 has three arms. An attempt with `ChallengeType == challengeType` and `WordPair == ""` fails arm 1 (`WordPair != ""`) and fails arm 2 (`ChallengeType != challengeType`), so it falls to `default` and is appended to `cold`. `_backfillLanglitAttempts` then hydrates the challenge and writes back `models.ExtractWordPair(challenge)`, which returns "" again (models/langlit_challenge.go:224-235 returns "" when no token carries an IncorrectForm) — the attempt is written with the exact same values and is cold again on the next request. The same holds for the `challenge == nil` branch at handlers.go:310-314, which deliberately leaves the attempt cold; `DeleteLanglitChallenge` exists at handlers.go:656, so deleted challenges are reachable.

This is doubled per request: `LanglitChallengeComponent` calls `ComputeProvenWordPairs` and then `ComputeSeenCorrectPairs`, and both run `_computeCorrectPairs` over the same slice. Warm attempts are deduped only because the first call mutates them in place — which is exactly what does not happen for this class.

The PR description's premise is "the data will be seamlessly upgraded and improve in performance over time". For this class it does the opposite: a permanent extra datastore read and an idempotent-but-repeated write on the student-facing challenge-fetch path, against a WrittenOnceModel. The models comment at langlit_challenge.go:308-312 already notes that "" is ambiguous; the code does not act on that.
claims.failure_scenario: A student attempts a word-pair challenge whose content has no IncorrectForm token (or whose challenge is later deleted): the attempt is stored with ChallengeType set but WordPair "", so every later challenge fetch re-classifies it as cold and re-issues GetMulti + PutMulti for it — twice per request, forever.

claims.label: suggestion (non-blocking)
claims.subject: The same "pairs to avoid" concept is implemented at two different thresholds on two paths, and the ≥1 `avoidPairs` set only takes effect on a cache miss — so the cached path, which returns early, can immediately repeat a pair the student just got right.
claims.discussion:
The same "pairs to avoid" concept is implemented at two different thresholds on two paths, and the ≥1 `avoidPairs` set only takes effect on a cache miss — so the cached path, which returns early, can immediately repeat a pair the student just got right. `GetUnseenChallenge` is called at langlit_challenge_component.go:854 and returns early whenever any unseen cached challenge exists, before the generation block at :964 that uses `avoidPairs`. So the ≥1 "seen correct" avoidance guards only the cache-miss path, while the ≥2 "proven" set guards only the cache-hit path. Since the cached path is the common one (it walks every page of matching challenges before falling through), `ComputeSeenCorrectPairs` is dead for most requests, yet it still costs a second full scan of `previousAttempts` and, when it does apply, a regeneration round.

The PR description sets the rubric at 2 corrects, so the cached path matches stated intent — but then the ≥1 set is a second, undeclared policy that fires only in the minority case. Either pass `avoidPairs` (or a soft-preference variant) into `GetUnseenChallenge` too, so both paths honor one policy, or drop the ≥1 tier and use `provenPairs` for the prompt as well. As written the two halves of the diff pull in different directions, and a reader cannot tell which threshold is the intended product behavior.

Related: `ComputeSeenCorrectPairs` is a strict superset of `ComputeProvenWordPairs` over identical counts — one pass returning both sets would remove the second scan and the implicit dependency on the first call's in-place mutation.
claims.failure_scenario: A student answers accept/except correctly once; on the next request `provenPairs` is empty (needs 2 corrects), `GetUnseenChallenge` filters nothing, and a cached unseen challenge using accept|except is returned and served before `avoidPairs` is ever consulted.

claims.discussion:
The pair-avoidance regeneration re-sends an identical prompt, so the retry adds a full extra LLM round trip on a student-facing path with no changed signal — despite the comment claiming the avoid list is "emphasized". Charging every cache-miss request for a coin-flip retry is a meaningful latency cost given the generation path already contains a 3-attempt dependency-generation loop nested inside it.

claims.label: suggestion (non-blocking)
claims.subject: The word_pair/challenge_type denormalization plus lazy backfill may be avoidable: the pair is derivable from the challenge, and the scope is small enough (≤25 attempts) to just GetMulti the challenges — is the saved read worth the migration machinery and the read-path write to a WrittenOnceModel?
claims.discussion: The word_pair/challenge_type denormalization plus lazy backfill may be avoidable: the pair is derivable from the challenge, and the scope is small enough (≤25 attempts) to just GetMulti the challenges — is the saved read worth the migration machinery and the read-path write to a WrittenOnceModel? The stated goal is "track word pairs"; the chosen mechanism is denormalizing `challenge_type` + `word_pair` onto `LanglitChallengeAttempt` so the computation can be done "without hydrating the challenge" (models/langlit_challenge.go:302-312). But the scope `_computeCorrectPairs` operates on is already bounded and small: assignment-scoped attempts, or `_provenScopeSize = 15` for unassigned practice — and this PR caps the practice-item config at 25 (langlit-*.json). The same request already does an unconditional `ctx.Datastore().GetMulti` of 5 challenge keys for noun extraction (langlit_challenge_component.go:890), and `_backfillLanglitAttempts` itself does a GetMulti of the cold challenges anyway (handlers.go:298) — so the warm path saves one batched key-get of ≤25 keys per request. The price is: a new datastore field with a two-state ("cold"/"warm") meaning, `_computeCorrectPairs`'s three-branch switch and its duplicate counting loop for the backfilled set, and a PutMulti on a GraphQL read/generation path. That write also fights the model's own declared contract: `LanglitChallengeAttempt.TransactionSafetyPolicy()` returns `datastore.WrittenOnceModel` (models/langlit_challenge.go:318), and the backfill only works by constructing fresh entities to clobber the stored ones — a workaround the code comment at handlers.go:278-280 documents rather than questions. Extracting pairs from a single batched challenge GetMulti over the scoped attempts would produce the same proven/seen sets with no schema change, no migration, no write amplification, and one code path instead of two.
claims.failure_scenario: The schema field, the lazy-migration path, and the cold/warm bifurcation are permanent surface area (~200 lines plus a datastore write on a read path) that a single batched key-get would have made unnecessary, and every future reader of the attempt model has to reason about the two-state field.
claims.suggestion: Compute pairs by batch-hydrating the scoped attempts' challenges (`models.MakeLanglitChallengeKey` + one `GetMulti`, exactly as `_backfillLanglitAttempts` already does) and calling `models.ExtractWordPair` in memory — dropping the `ChallengeType`/`WordPair` datastore fields, `_backfillLanglitAttempts`, and the cold/warm branching entirely. Keep the resolver-side write only if a later, larger scope makes the read genuinely expensive.

claims.label: question (non-blocking)
claims.subject: The avoid list uses ≥1 correct while the stated rubric is 2 corrects — for a pair first seen on the generation path, doesn't ≥1 make the second correct unreachable and so prevent the pair from ever becoming proven?
claims.discussion: The avoid list uses ≥1 correct while the stated rubric is 2 corrects — for a pair first seen on the generation path, doesn't ≥1 make the second correct unreachable and so prevent the pair from ever becoming proven? The PR body states the rubric plainly: "we use 2 correct attempts on a word pair as a rubric", and `_masteryThreshold = 2` (handlers.go:32) encodes it for the cached path. But `ComputeSeenCorrectPairs` passes `1` (handlers.go:177), and that ≥1 list is what feeds `{avoidPairs}` into the generation prompt and the regen check. The code comment at langlit_challenge_component.go:831-835 justifies ≥1 as "not re-showing a pair the student just got right" and accounts for one cost (pushing the model to rarer pairs) — but not for this one: both lists are computed over the *same* scope, so within an assignment a pair with exactly 1 correct is excluded from generation while remaining eligible from cache. The generation path only runs when `GetUnseenChallenge` returns nil (line 865-868), i.e. precisely when no cached challenge is available. So for a pair whose only occurrence came from generation, the second correct required by the rubric can only arrive if the cache happens to hold a matching unseen challenge; otherwise the pair is stuck at 1 forever, never enters `provenPairs`, and the proven filter never fires for it. Was ≥1 vs ≥2 for the avoid list a deliberate split, or should the avoid list also be the ≥2 proven set (which would make the two paths agree and let a pair actually reach mastery)?
claims.failure_scenario: A pair a student answers correctly once on the generation path can never earn its second correct there, so it never becomes "proven" and the 2-correct mastery signal the whole feature is built on is unreachable for those pairs.

claims.label: thought (non-blocking)
claims.subject: The one-shot regeneration re-sends an identical prompt after the full dependency-generation chain has already run, so it is a pure re-roll rather than a stronger instruction — is one extra full pipeline worth it?
claims.discussion: The one-shot regeneration re-sends an identical prompt after the full dependency-generation chain has already run, so it is a pure re-roll rather than a stronger instruction — is one extra full pipeline worth it? The loop comment at lines 955-960 says "regenerate with the avoid list emphasized" (line 1066 repeats it), but the second iteration builds the same `map[string]string` with the same `"avoidPairs": strings.Join(avoidPairs, ", ")` (line 978) — nothing is emphasized, escalated, or narrowed. The model already had the avoid list on the first pass and ignored it; an identical prompt gives roughly the same odds again. The cost is not small: the pair is only extractable from `dependencyGenerationOutput` (`ExtractWordPairFromText`, line 1059), so the check at line 1058 sits *after* the inner `depGenMaxRetries = 3` loop, and a regen throws away one sentence generation, one classification, and up to three dependency-generation calls. Either the second pass should differ from the first in a way that actually changes the outcome (e.g. drop the losing pair into a hard exclusion, or shrink the candidate space), or the re-roll could be dropped and the model's first answer accepted — the code already treats repetition as an acceptable degradation once the budget is spent (line 1063-1065).
claims.failure_scenario: A regeneration discards a completed generate + classify + up-to-3-dependency-generation chain and re-runs all of it with a byte-identical prompt, roughly doubling worst-case latency on a student-facing request for a re-roll whose only new information is chance.

The three-arm switch at handlers.go:221-231 does classify a warm attempt with ChallengeType == challengeType and WordPair == "" into `default`, and _backfillLanglitAttempts writes back models.ExtractWordPair(challenge) which returns "" again (models/langlit_challenge.go:224-235) — so the attempt is re-Put identically each request; the doubling is real too, since langlit_challenge_component.go:821 and 836 both run _computeCorrectPairs over the same slice.

langlit_challenge_component.go:865-868 returns early on any cached unseen challenge, before avoidPairs is used at 978 — so the ≥1 seen-correct set only affects the cache-miss path while the ≥2 proven set only filters the cache path, and ComputeSeenCorrectPairs (836) still pays a second full scan of previousAttempts on every request; the stated scenario (one correct → provenPairs empty → cached challenge repeats the pair) follows directly.

The design tradeoff is arguable, but two of its supports do not hold up: the 5-key noun-extraction GetMulti at langlit_challenge_component.go:890 sits after the cache-hit early return at 865-868, so it is not 'unconditional' and the cache-hit path would need a new GetMulti under the proposed alternative; and the fresh-entity write is sanctioned framework behavior (pkg/gcloud/datastore/transaction_safety_test.go:679 TestWrittenOnceModelCanBeClobbered), not a policy workaround. The core cost/complexity question is still legitimate, so I kept it with the inaccurate supports removed.

corrected.subject: Is the word_pair/challenge_type denormalization plus lazy backfill worth it, given the scope is already ≤25 attempts and derivable from the challenge?
corrected.discussion:
Is the word_pair/challenge_type denormalization plus lazy backfill worth it, given the scope is already ≤25 attempts and derivable from the challenge? The stated goal is "track word pairs"; the chosen mechanism denormalizes `challenge_type` + `word_pair` onto `LanglitChallengeAttempt` so the computation can run "without hydrating the challenge" (models/langlit_challenge.go:302-312). But the scope `_computeCorrectPairs` works over is already bounded and small: assignment-scoped attempts, or `_provenScopeSize = 15` for unassigned practice — and this PR caps the teacher-facing practice-item option at 25.

The alternative would be to batch-hydrate the scoped attempts' challenges (`models.MakeLanglitChallengeKey` + one `GetMulti`, exactly what `_backfillLanglitAttempts` already does at handlers.go:293-302) and call `models.ExtractWordPair` in memory. That costs one batched key-get of ≤25 keys per request — including on the cache-hit path, which today pays nothing. What it buys is dropping the new datastore fields, the two-state cold/warm meaning, the three-branch switch plus its duplicate counting loop, and a `PutMulti` on a read path.

Worth stating explicitly which side of that trade you intended, since the migration machinery is permanent surface area every future reader of the attempt model has to reason about.
corrected.suggestion: Compute pairs by batch-hydrating the scoped attempts' challenges (`models.MakeLanglitChallengeKey` + one `GetMulti`) and calling `models.ExtractWordPair` in memory — dropping the `ChallengeType`/`WordPair` datastore fields, `_backfillLanglitAttempts`, and the cold/warm branching entirely. Keep the denormalization only if the ≤25-key get on the cache-hit path is judged too expensive.

claims.reason: The stated mechanism does not hold: langlit_challenge_component.go:1063-1065 relaxes after `pairAvoidMaxRegens = 1` and accepts a pair that is on the avoid list, so a seen-once pair can still be generated and served on the generation path; and the cached path is unfiltered for it too, since GetUnseenChallenge only skips `provenPairs` (≥2) at handlers.go:411-414. A pair with exactly one correct is therefore reachable from both paths, so it is not 'stuck at 1 forever' and mastery is not unreachable. (The related, real observation — that the ≥1 and ≥2 tiers apply to different paths — is already carried by holistic-2.)

Verified the placement mismatch: `ReconstructSentence` and `ReconstructIncorrectSentence` are methods on *UniversalDependencyText in models/universal_dependency_types.go:53 and 74, while the new `ExtractWordPairFromText(t *UniversalDependencyText)` is a free function in langlit_challenge.go:224 whose tests were added to universal_dependency_types_test.go. A placement preference, not a rule — kept as a minor suggestion.

The constant's only read is handlers.go:211 inside the shared `_computeCorrectPairs`, and ComputeSeenCorrectPairs routes through it at handlers.go:177, so the `_proven`-scoped name and doc comment (handlers.go:21-25) do under-describe what the window governs; the root CLAUDE.md rule quoted ("Name a function for what it actually does and the scope it covers") is real, though it is stated for functions rather than constants.

The comment exists verbatim at handlers.go:409-410 ("provenPairs is empty for non-FCW types, so this filter is a / no-op there."), and the only caller computes provenPairs whenever `wordPairType` holds — FCW, apostrophe usage, or SVA (langlit_challenge_component.go:808-810, 814-826) — so the filter is live for two of the three types the comment says it is inert for.

Both comments exist verbatim at handlers.go:215-217 and 227 and say FCW/non-FCW, while the code compares against the caller-supplied `challengeType` parameter at 222 and 226; the diff's own tests (TestComputeProvenWordPairs_ApostropheCounted, TestComputeSeenCorrectPairs_SubjectVerbAgreement) exercise the loop for apostrophe and SVA.

The field comments exist verbatim at models/langlit_challenge.go:302-311 and scope both sentences to FCW, but the consumer `_computeCorrectPairs` is parameterized by `challengeType` and its cold branch (handlers.go:228-231) treats an empty WordPair as needing migration for every type, not just FCW.
